newsitem.title: ITALY: POLL - Italian yields seen converging further on EMU.
newsitem.headline: POLL - Italian yields seen converging further on EMU.

text.p: Italian yields will converge with Germany on rising optimism that Italy will catch the EMU train while inflation, up to now the focus of Bank of Italy monetary policy, moves into the background, economists polled by Reuters said.

A quarterly survey of 16 analysts, carried out from June 30 to July 2, indicated a median spread for the 10-year Italian Btp bond over the benchmark Bund gradually narrowing from a current 100 basis points to 90 bps at end-1997 and 60 bps at end-1998.
On Wednesday July 9, after several trading sessions on the futures market saw Btp prices set one record high after another, the spread touched a new historic low of 91 basis points.
The 16 economists generally saw Italy's key discount rate remaining steady at 6.25 percent until the end of the third quarter and then falling half a point by December.
The Bank of Italy is then seen gradually reducing the rate to 4.5 percent by the end of 1998. The central bank last cut the rate by 50 basis points from 6.75 percent on June 30.
For Renzo Avesani, head of Risk Management at Cariplo, "the convergence process is well and truly underway and there are no major obstacles preventing a cut in rates."

Cariplo saw a bond spread of 100 bps at the end of the current quarter, narrowing to 70 bps by the end of next year, with a discount rate steady at 6.25 percent and then being reduced to 5.0 percent at end-1998.
The bank saw an inflation rate of 1.9 percent at end-1997 and of 2.0 percent at end-1998.
Italian June CPI came in at a year on year 1.4 percent, a 28-year low, after 1.6 percent rate in May, but many analysts saw inflation starting to turn up slightly from the June trough.
"The rise in inflation is not worrying and should not be an impediment to a cut in rates," Avesani said.
Analysts saw average 1997 inflation at 1.9 percent, below the government's targeted 2.5 percent, and at 2.3 percent in 1998, above the official 1.8 percent goal.
Gianluca Sanna, analyst at Stone & McCarthy said, "inflation is no longer a factor which is guiding monetary policy.

"The Bank of Italy is looking at the entire process which will take Italy into European economic and monetary union, including possible international upsets, and is also closely watching the process of Italian welfare state reform which is still only moving along very slowly," Sanna said.
He noted that central bank governor Antonio Fazio has made abundantly clear his concern about the need for durable structural and social reforms.

He added, "If one accepts the idea EMU will start on time with Italy then one must also reckon that in a year from now the spread between Italian and German yields will just reflect the credit risk and therefore will be around 30 to 50 basis points."
"We see the 10-year Italian Btp bond yielding 6.20 percent in mid-1998, some 30 to 40 bps above the Bund. This is the goal, the route taken to get there is less important," Sanna said.
On Wednesday, the February 2007 Btp was yielding around 6.46 percent.
"In coming months I think all the doubts over a possible delay to the EMU start will fade away and so rates will continue to fall," said Sanna who saw the discount rate at 5.0 percent in mid-1998.

HSBC, however, considering the market over optimistic about Italy being in the first wave of EMU, forecast the bond spread at 135 bps at the end of the current quarter, narrowing to 80 bps at end-1998. But HSBC did see the discount rate being reduced to 4.5 percent by the end of next year.

"I think that in autumn there will be confirmation of the accord between Germany and France on the need for sustainable fiscal measures, and not only on the achievement of the Maastricht criteria. I think there will be a modest correction of the Btp/Bund spread on this," said Ros Lifton of HSBC.
